title: How will you optimize a slow query (EXPLAIN, indexing, rewrite, proper joins, avoid functions on indexed columns, partitioning, caching, schema, server resources)?
shortTitle: How will you optimize a slow query
keyPoints: Always start with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to see the actual execution plan with real timings and row counts before making any changes.
A large gap between estimated and actual rows means stale statistics; running `ANALYZE` on the table to refresh them is sometimes the entire fix.
Indexing is the most common fix: add a composite index matching the filter with equality columns first and range columns last.
Make predicates sargable by removing functions from indexed columns so the index can be used by the query planner.
Ensure both sides of a join are indexed on the join key so the planner can choose an efficient hash or merge join.
Partitioning, caching, denormalization, and schema changes are heavier measures reserved for when indexing and rewriting are insufficient.
Change one thing at a time and re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE after every change, because stacking fixes blindly hides what actually helped.

s1_definition.oneliner: Read the plan first, fix the dominant cost with the least invasive change (index, rewrite, join, sargability), escalate to partitioning, caching, schema, or hardware only if needed, and re-check the plan every time.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Measure first** – Always start with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to capture the actual execution plan with real timings and row counts, never guess.
- **Least invasive fix** – Apply the cheapest effective change first: refresh statistics, add or adjust indexes, rewrite predicates to be sargable, choose proper join strategies.
- **Escalate when needed** – Only after exhausting indexing and rewriting consider partitioning, caching, schema changes, or more server resources.
- **Re-measure always** – After each change, re-run the plan to confirm the improvement rather than assuming it worked.
s1_definition.analogy: When a National Bank of India report is slow, you do not randomly throw more hardware at it. You first ask the database to show its work: a step-by-step replay of how it found the answer. That replay reveals the real culprit: maybe the clerk read the entire ledger instead of using the index. You fix exactly that, and only if the data is genuinely enormous do you split it into yearly volumes (partitioning) or keep popular answers on a sticky note (caching). After each fix you ask for the replay again to confirm it got faster.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Optimizing a slow query is a disciplined, measure-first process, never guesswork. The very first step is always `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to get the actual plan with real timings and real row counts. That immediately tells you where the time goes: a sequential scan on a big table, a nested loop over too many rows, a sort spilling to disk, or a big gap between estimated and actual rows that signals stale statistics.

From there, apply the cheapest effective change. Indexing is the most common fix: a composite index matching the filter with equality columns first and range columns last. Then rewrite for logical cost: make predicates sargable by removing functions from indexed columns, select only the columns you need instead of star, and ensure both join sides are indexed. Only when the data itself is genuinely huge do you reach for heavier tools: range partitioning so queries prune to one slice, caching for hot read-mostly results, or schema changes like pre-aggregated summary tables.

The critical discipline is to change one thing at a time and re-run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` after every change, because stacking fixes blindly makes it impossible to know what actually helped. Hardware upgrades are the last resort because they hide an inefficient query rather than fixing it.

At the National Bank of India, the account-statement query ran for eight seconds. The plan showed a sequential scan over ten million rows plus a disk sort. Rajesh refreshed statistics, added a composite index on account and date, and the plan turned into an index range scan with the sort node gone, dropping the query to under one millisecond.

Remember one sentence: read the plan first, fix the dominant cost with the least invasive change, and re-check the plan every time.
